deep.reconstruction:
This page has no mathematics. It is a letter in German Kurrent script, dated 'Göttingen 26. März 1875' and signed 'Wöhler'. The writer is almost certainly the chemist Friedrich Wöhler, then in Göttingen. The addressee ('Hochzuverehrender Herr Professor') is almost certainly Heinrich Weber, who was preparing Riemann's Gesammelte mathematische Werke (1876). There is a pencil folio number '84' at the upper right.

Content, paraphrased:
(1) Wöhler sends Weber the original manuscript of Riemann's Abhandlung, borrowed from the Paris Académie des Sciences. He is pleased that the request succeeded and that Weber thereby gains an important contribution to his undertaking, i.e. the edition.
(2) He encloses a letter from the Académie. This is the French letter on the previous page, signed 'pour le Secrétaire perpétuel'. It shows that lending the manuscript was really against the Académie's regulations. The concession is owed to J.-B. Dumas, secrétaire perpétuel.
(3) Wöhler has already thanked Dumas. He suggests Weber also express his gratitude after the manuscript has been returned.
(4) After use, the manuscript should be returned directly to the Académie.
(5) If the Abhandlung is printed in full, it would be fitting to send the Académie a copy.
(6) He asks Weber to confirm receipt.

The manuscript in question is Riemann's 1861 Paris prize essay on heat conduction, the 'Commentatio mathematica, qua respondere tentatur quaestioni ab Illma Academia Parisiensi propositae'. That essay treats the problem of when a quadratic differential form can be transformed into one with constant coefficients, and introduces what are now the Riemann curvature quantities. Weber did print it in full in the Werke (1876). This explains why the letter sits in the 'Waermeleitung' bundle. No derivation exists on this page to reconstruct.

results.what: Archival/provenance information: the original manuscript of Riemann's 1861 Paris prize essay on heat conduction (Commentatio mathematica) was lent by the Académie des Sciences, through Wöhler and with Dumas's concession, to H. Weber in March 1875 for the Gesammelte Werke edition; it was to be returned directly to Paris.
results.modern_name: Provenance of the text of the Commentatio mathematica (Riemann, Werke 1876, item XXII)
results.usually_credited_to: N/A (editorial history; Weber's edition notes the text came from the Paris manuscript)

deep.surprise_reason: This is an editorial cover letter by Wöhler, not Riemann, with no mathematical content. It documents the already known fact that Weber obtained the Paris prize essay from the Académie for the 1876 Werke. Details such as Dumas's concession against the regulations and the request to send a printed copy are minor archival color.
transcription_corrections: The page is a letter in Wöhler's hand, not a Riemann manuscript. The signature 'Wöhler' and the date 'Göttingen 26. März 1875' match the image.
The interlinear insertion 'sende' above the end of line 1 ('Riemann's Abhandlung sende') is confirmed by the image.
The interlinear insertion 'war' above 'Academie' ('gegen das Reglement der Academie war') is confirmed.
'des Sciences' is written in the left margin, continuing 'secrétaire perpétuel de l'Académie' from the line above. The transcription correctly joins it.
'ich dächte aber es würde wohl passend sein' is uncertain in the hand. A reading such as 'ich dächte aber es wäre wohl passend' is possible, though the sense is unaffected.
There is a pencil folio number '84' at the upper right that the transcription omits.
Next-page note: the mirror-image date is more likely the reverse of a related letter (possibly from Weber) and should not be read as '185?'. This is unverifiable from this image.
